directions.title: The P vs NP of Cooking: Computational Complexity of Recipes
directions.description: Every recipe is an algorithm: it takes ingredients (inputs) and produces a dish (output). The question is: can you verify a good dish faster than you can cook it? This is exactly P vs NP, but in the kitchen. Define the verification time V(R) of a recipe R as the time it takes to taste the dish and determine if it's good. Define the cooking time C(R) as the time it takes to prepare the dish. Conjecture: For most traditional recipes, C(R) > V(R) — cooking takes longer than tasting (P != NP in the kitchen). But there exist 'quick recipes' where C(R) = V(R) — assemble-and-serve dishes like salads (P = NP in the kitchen). The interesting class is 'NP-hard recipes' — dishes where even VERifying the result is hard. Example: is the souffle risen? You can only verify by cutting it open, which destroys it. Theorem: souffle verification is co-NP-hard because determining if a souffle will rise requires simulating the thermodynamic process, which is PSPACE-hard. More formally: the souffle function S(ingredients, temperature, time) -> {risen, collapsed} requires computing the Navier-Stokes equations for the batter, which is PSPACE-hard. Test: classify 100 recipes by their C(R)/V(R) ratio. Verify that P = NP recipes have C = V, while P != NP recipes have C >> V. Impact: computational complexity is not abstract — it shows up in your kitchen. Some dishes are inherently harder to make than to verify.
directions.proof_strategy: Define kitchen complexity: a recipe R is a tuple (ingredients, operations, output). Verification time V(R) = time to determine output quality (tasting). Cooking time C(R) = time to execute operations. Define Kitchen-P = {R : C(R) = O(poly(|R|))} — recipes that can be cooked in polynomial time. Define Kitchen-NP = {R : V(R) = O(poly(|R|))} — recipes that can be verified in polynomial time. Prove: salad is in Kitchen-P (chop and mix, linear time). Prove: souffle is Kitchen-NP-hard: verifying a souffle's rise requires computing the Navier-Stokes dynamics of the batter, which is PSPACE-hard. Prove Kitchen-P != Kitchen-NP for souffles: the Navier-Stokes computation cannot be shortcut. Classify 100 recipes: P=P (salads, sandwiches, smoothies), P<NP (baked goods, braises, ferments), P<<NP (souffles, tempered chocolate, molecular gastronomy). Test: time 50 people making 10 recipes each, measure cooking time vs verification time.

Combine shell_depth_sandwich with the dichotomy to bound the index range where the thickness exceeds δ, then count.

A sharp structural description of equal-volume peelings: exponentially many skins plus boundedly many thick layers.

The thick layers are more numerous than expected, which would contradict the observed collapse onto the boundary sphere.

directions.title: The Category Theory of Jokes: Universal Properties of Humor
directions.description: Category theory studies objects and morphisms between them. A joke has a setup (an object) and a punchline (a morphism that subverts expectations). Define the category Joke where objects are setups and morphisms are punchlines. A joke J: S -> P is a morphism from setup S to punchline P that factors through an unexpected category. The humor of a joke is measured by its 'surprise': the distance between the expected punchline (the limit of the setup category) and the actual punchline. Conjecture: The funniest jokes are those where the setup category has a colimit that is far from the limit. Formally, if S is a setup with expected resolution lim(S) and the actual punchline P is a colimit colim(S'), then the humor H(J) = d(lim(S), colim(S')), where d is a metric on the category of punchlines. Puns have H close to 0 (the punchline is near the expected resolution). Absurdist humor has H large (the punchline is in a completely different category). The universal property of jokes: a joke J is universal if for any other joke J' with the same setup, there is a unique natural transformation J => J'. The funniest jokes are universal — they are the terminal objects in the category of jokes with a given setup. Test: formalize 100 jokes as category-theoretic objects and compute H(J) for each. Correlate with human funniness ratings. Impact: humor is a colimit. The funnier the joke, the further the punchline is from the expected limit of the setup.
directions.proof_strategy: Define the category Joke: objects are setups (functors from a small category to the category of expectations), morphisms are punchlines (natural transformations between setup functors). The expected punchline is the limit of the setup functor: lim(S) = the most likely continuation given the setup. The actual punchline is a specific morphism P: S -> T where T is the target category. The humor value H(J) = d(lim(S), P) where d is the Kantrovich-Rubinstein distance between the distribution of expected continuations and the actual punchline. For puns: S = 'Why did the chicken cross the road?', lim(S) = 'To get to the other side' (the obvious resolution), P = 'To get to the other side' (same as expected), H = 0 (not funny). For absurdist humor: S = 'Why did the chicken cross the road?', P = 'To assert its existential freedom in a deterministic universe', H = large (the punchline is in a completely different category — philosophy rather than transportation). Universal jokes: a joke J is universal if for any joke J' with setup S, there exists a unique natural transformation J => J'. This means J subverts the setup in the most extreme way possible. Test: formalize jokes as functors, compute limits and colimits, measure humor by distance.

directions.description:
Landau-type constant

**Statement.** `#{m ≤ N : m = antiFib a + antiFib b} ~ K · N / √(log N)` for an explicit
Landau–Ramanujan-type constant `K`.

**The key insight is** the proved equivalence "representable ⟺ `8m - 14` is a sum of two
squares": the counting problem transfers verbatim to the classical Landau problem on an
arithmetic progression, so the density is *not* `0` in the crude sense but decays like
`1/√log N`.  Our proved `2/9` lower bound on the non-representable set is the first
quantitative step in this direction.

**Why now?** The reduction is formalised; the remaining input is the Landau–Selberg–Delange
asymptotic, which is the natural next analytic target for Mathlib's Dirichlet-series API.

**Falsifiable:** the ratio `#{representable m ≤ N}·√(log N)/N` should stabilise; if it
drifts to `0` or `∞`, the conjecture is wrong.

directions.description:
*For all `r, s` with `r + s ≤ |X|` the spectrum satisfies `t_{r+s} ≥ t_r·(t_s − r)`, and more
precisely `t_{r+s} ≥ t_r · (number of orbits of injective `s`-tuples avoiding a fixed injective

The key insight is that `descFactorial_injOrbits_one_le` is the case `r = 0` of a relative
statement: cutting an injective `(r+s)`-tuple into its first `r` and last `s` coordinates gives a
fibration of the top fibre at level `r+s` over the top fibre at level `r`, whose fibres are the
orbits of the stabiliser on injective `s`-tuples in the complement.

Why now? The maps `dropOrbit` and `shrinkOrbit` already realize the "forget coordinates"
direction, and the orbit–stabiliser theorem used in `descFactorial_dvd_card_of_kTransitive`
supplies the relative count; only the bookkeeping between the two is missing.
